questions.question: Explain how a beam carries load across a gap, why a deep beam is stiffer than a wide one, and how the I-beam shape saves material.
questions.expected_answer: A beam rests on supports at both ends and carries load by bending: the load pushes the middle down, the top surface is compressed and the bottom stretched, and the supports push up at the ends. Depth matters because the top and bottom fibres resist bending more the further they are from the beam's centre line, so a plank on its edge is far stiffer than the same plank flat. Since the top and bottom do most of the work, the I-beam keeps wide flanges top (compression) and bottom (tension) and thins the middle to a web that carries shear, giving nearly the stiffness of a solid beam with a fraction of the steel.

questions.question: Compare a suspension bridge with a cable-stayed bridge: how each hangs its deck, which members are in tension and compression, and an example.
questions.expected_answer: Suspension: two main cables drape from shore anchorages over two towers; vertical hangers drop to the deck. Main cables and hangers are in tension, towers in compression, and massive anchorages resist the cable pull; suits the longest spans (over 1000 m), e.g. the Golden Gate Bridge. Cable-stayed: cables run straight from the deck to one or more towers like harp strings, with no draped cable or shore anchorages; stays in tension, towers in compression, deck also compressed along its length; suits 200-1000 m and is cheaper there, e.g. the Nelson Mandela Bridge in Johannesburg.

questions.question: Describe how an arch and a cantilever each carry load, state the condition each needs at its supports, and give an example of each.
questions.expected_answer: An arch carries load in compression only: the curve leads load down and outward to abutments at each end, so stone, brick or plain concrete can be used; the abutments must be heavy or founded in rock to resist the outward thrust, e.g. the Bloukrans Bridge concrete arch. A cantilever is fixed at one end only and carries load by bending from its root, where bending is greatest, with tension on top and compression underneath; the root must be firmly clamped and usually counterbalanced by the floor or wall, e.g. a balcony, a diving board or a tower crane jib.
